sections.body:
A tooth is a strong little tool that sits in your jaw. It cuts and chews the food you eat. Every person has twenty baby teeth, and then most adults have thirty-two teeth.

The part you can see is called the **crown**. It is covered with **enamel**, the hardest substance in your whole body. Enamel is even harder than bone. It has to be, because teeth take a lot of biting and chewing.

Under the crown is the **dentin**. Dentin is softer than enamel, and it makes up most of the tooth. Inside the dentin runs the **pulp**, which holds the blood vessels and the nerves. That is why a deep hole in a tooth can hurt so much.

Roots hold the tooth in the jaw. They sit inside the gum, and they are surrounded by a soft layer called **cementum**.

Teeth are not alone in your mouth. Around each tooth there is a small pocket of gum. The gum makes a seal that keeps food from slipping underneath the tooth. It is a good seal, but it is not perfect, and that is where trouble starts.

Your mouth is warm and damp, and it is full of tiny germs. The germs feed on the bits of food that stay on your teeth. They make acid, the acid softens the enamel, and a hole begins to grow. That hole is called a **cavity**. Brushing is how you stop it.
examples: Enamel is the hardest part of your body, and it covers the crown.
The pulp holds the nerves, and that is why a deep hole hurts.
The gum makes a seal that keeps food from slipping under the tooth.
sections.heading: What a Tooth Is Made Of

sections.body:
Every tooth is under attack, all day long. Here is how it happens.

First, your mouth is full of germs. They are too small to see. Some of them are harmless, but some of them like sugar very much.

When you eat or drink something with sugar in it, the germs eat the sugar too. While they do this, they make **acid**. The acid is the real enemy, not the sugar itself.

The acid is strong enough to soften the enamel on your tooth. It dissolves a tiny layer of the hardest substance in your body.

Now you have a **plaque** on your tooth. Plaque is a soft, sticky film of germs and food. It forms in the small pocket around the tooth and right along the gum line.

Every time you eat, the plaque gets more acid, and the enamel loses a bit more. If you clean the plaque away, the enamel can heal itself. That is the good news.

But if the plaque stays, the hole keeps growing. It grows into the dentin, and dentin is softer, so the hole gets bigger faster. Then the germs can reach the pulp, and the tooth starts to hurt. That is how a small hole becomes a big one.

Snacks that sit on your teeth for a long time make it worse. That is why a biscuit eaten slowly at a party does more harm than the same biscuit at dinner with a brush afterwards.
examples: The germs make acid, and the acid is the real enemy.
Plaque is a soft, sticky film of germs and food on your tooth.
If the plaque stays, the hole keeps growing.
sections.heading: How Sugar Makes Holes in Teeth

sections.body:
Brushing does two jobs. It scrapes the plaque off, and it cleans the enamel so the acid has nothing to sit on.

The toothbrush bristles do the scraping. They reach the edges of the teeth and the gum line, where the plaque collects.

Toothpaste does the rest. It has **fluoride** in it, and fluoride makes the enamel tougher. It also helps the enamel repair small damage. This is why dentists always ask which toothpaste you use.

Brushing also changes what happens to the sugar. While you brush, you are removing the food that the germs were eating. The germs have less to work on, so they make less acid.

And here is a good habit that surprises people. Saliva, the wet stuff in your mouth, helps repair enamel. It works best when there is no plaque to sit in the way. So a clean mouth heals better than a dirty one.

Brushing cannot fix a hole that is already there. Only a dentist can do that. Brushing stops holes from starting, and that is the whole job.
examples: The bristles scrape the plaque off the tooth.
Fluoride in toothpaste makes the enamel tougher.
Brushing stops holes from starting, but only a dentist can fill one.
sections.heading: How Brushing Stops the Holes

sections.body:
These are the words you will need when you talk about your teeth.

Enamel is the hard outer coat of a tooth. It is the hardest part of your body.

Dentin is the softer layer under the enamel. It makes up most of the tooth.

Plaque is a soft, sticky film of germs and food that gathers on your teeth.

A **cavity** is a hole in a tooth. It forms when acid from plaque weakens the enamel.

Gums are the soft flesh that holds your teeth in place and protects them.

A **dentist** is a doctor who looks after teeth. A **hygienist** is the person who cleans them.

Fluoride is a mineral in toothpaste. It makes the enamel stronger against acid.

sections.body:
Most people brush too fast, and they miss the same teeth every time. Here is a way that works.

Take a pea-sized amount of toothpaste with fluoride. That is about right for a grown-up, and a rice-grain amount for a small child.

Start at the back of the mouth, on the inside of your teeth. Many people skip this because they cannot see it. Give it a little more time than the rest.

Brush in small circles, not side to side. Let the bristles go between the teeth, at the edge of the gum.

Brush the outside of your teeth, then the inside, then the chewing surfaces at the back. Do the same for the top, the bottom and the back.

Do not forget your tongue. It holds germs too, and it is often left behind.

Spit, but do not rinse with a big mouthful of water. The leftover fluoride is what helps your teeth most. Just spit out the toothpaste.

Brush for about two minutes. A good way to time it is to hum a slow song that lasts two minutes.

And brush twice a day, in the morning and before bed. The night one is the most important, because that is when your saliva slows down and the germs have the longest time to work.
examples: I start at the back because that is where I miss most.
I brush in little circles, not side to side.
I brush twice a day, and the night one is the most important.
sections.heading: How to Brush Your Teeth Well
steps: Take a pea-sized amount of toothpaste with fluoride.
Start at the back of the mouth on the inside of the teeth.
Brush in small circles, letting the bristles go between the teeth.
Brush the outside, then the inside, then the chewing surfaces.
Spit out the toothpaste without rinsing with water.

sections.body:
Not all snacks are equal. Here is how to pick ones that do less harm.

Snacks that are sticky and sugary are the worst. They stick to the tooth and feed the germs for a long time. Toffee, chewing gum with sugar, and dried fruit are all sticky.

Snacks that are sour are also tricky. Lemon and sweets that fizz feel sharp on the tongue, and the acid softens the enamel for a while afterwards.

Snacks that are hard are risky in a different way. A hard sweet or a bone can crack a tooth.

Better choices are cheese, plain yoghurt, apples, carrots and nuts. They are not sweet, and they make you chew, and chewing saliva helps your teeth.

Water is the best drink between meals. It washes food away and it does not feed the germs at all. Milk is a good drink with meals, because it has calcium, which is good for teeth.

And if a tooth hurts, or if a tooth feels funny when you bite on it, tell an adult. Do not wait. Small problems are easy to fix, and the dentist would much rather see you early.
examples: Cheese and apples are kinder to my teeth than toffee.
Water is better than juice between meals.
My tooth feels funny, so I will tell my mum today.
sections.heading: Snacks That Are Kinder to Your Teeth

item.summary: Brushing feels normal, but teeth are in real danger every single day. After reading this, you can explain what plaque does to a tooth, brush properly, and pick snacks that are kinder to your teeth.
item.title: Why Do We Brush Our Teeth?
